strengths: An intriguing conceptual idea to repurpose TabPFN—a prior-data fitted network originally meta-trained for tabular supervised tasks—as a gradient-free Q-function regressor within Fitted Q Iteration (FQI).

Clear qualitative identification of the theoretical mismatch between TabPFN's pre-training assumptions (i.i.d. data, static targets) and the RL setup (non-i.i.d. trajectories, non-stationary policy-induced distributions, bootstrapped Bellman targets).
Systematic ablation of context management strategies and hyperparameter sensitivity (e.g., initial epsilon, epsilon decay, refit thresholds, context budget).
weaknesses: Severely limited empirical scope: Experiments are restricted to only three low-dimensional classic control benchmarks (CartPole-v1, MountainCar-v0, Acrobot-v1). No continuous control tasks (e.g., Pendulum, MuJoCo/Gymnasium continuous control) or slightly larger environments were attempted.

Reliance on heavy reward shaping: As admitted in the text and detailed in the Appendix, standard sparse/default rewards failed, requiring custom dense reward shaping for all three environments (e.g., distance/velocity shaping for MountainCar, end-effector height for Acrobot). This significantly diminishes the generality and autonomy expected of reinforcement learning algorithms.

Lack of competitive and representative baselines: The method is only compared against a basic DQN implementation. Standard gradient-free baselines (e.g., CMA-ES, genetic algorithms, ARS) as well as modern RL methods (PPO, SAC, TD3) or linear/kernel FQI methods are absent.

Unsubstantiated computational efficiency claims: The paper claims TabPFN-RL is 'computationally efficient' and 'fast', yet provides no wall-clock time or computational complexity comparison against DQN or other baselines. Given that TabPFN-FQI performs 60 full iterations of transformer forward passes over contexts of hundreds or thousands of tokens whenever an episode passes the gating threshold, the actual wall-clock cost is likely substantial.

The 'theoretical' contributions are purely descriptive: Section 'TabPFN-RL and Task-Prior Mismatch' and 'Theoretical Limitations' state well-known qualitative facts (e.g., finite context windows fill up, RL transitions violate i.i.d. assumptions) without providing formal bounds, error analysis, or convergence proofs under model-induced Bellman error.

strengths: Creative conceptual exploration: Repurposing a prior-data fitted network (TabPFN) as a non-parametric Q-function regressor within Fitted Q Iteration (FQI) is an interesting and novel angle for gradient-free reinforcement learning.

Insightful discussion of prior mismatch: The paper transparently discusses the theoretical disconnect between TabPFN's meta-training assumption (i.i.d. tabular data) and RL dynamics (bootstrapped non-stationary Bellman targets, correlated trajectory transitions, and policy-induced state visitation drift).

Identification of context limitations: The authors explicitly address the finite context bottleneck inherent to in-context RL methods and propose heuristic truncation/filtering strategies (e.g., naive deduplication) to enable continual interaction.
weaknesses: Extremely limited and unconvincing empirical evaluation: Experiments are restricted to three trivial classic control environments (CartPole-v1, MountainCar-v0, and Acrobot-v1). Crucially, the method completely fails under standard environmental rewards and relies heavily on hand-crafted dense reward shaping functions across all three environments, which severely diminishes the significance of the results.

Lack of critical baselines: TabPFN is evaluated only against standard DQN. Because TabPFN-FQI is fundamentally a tabular/non-parametric regressor applied to Fitted Q Iteration, the paper should compare against standard FQI baselines (e.g., Tree-based FQI with ExtraTrees/Random Forests or Gradient Boosted Trees, as well as KNN-based regressors) to demonstrate whether TabPFN's learned prior provides any tangible benefit over established tabular regression methods.

Unsupported computational efficiency claims: The paper frequently claims that the method is 'fast and computationally efficient' because it sidesteps backpropagation. However, TabPFN incurs quadratic attention complexity $O(B^2)$ with respect to context size $B$, and running full transformer inference across dozens of FQI iterations (the appendix reports 60 FQI iterations) per episode or update is computationally demanding compared to a lightweight DQN MLP. The paper provides no wall-clock time, GPU memory, or FLOP comparisons.

Heuristic nature of context truncation without theoretical backing: While framed under 'Theoretical Limitations', the continual learning analysis consists entirely of simple empirical heuristics (L, ND, ED, RV) without formal convergence, error bounds, or regret guarantees. Furthermore, context truncation is evaluated only on a single shaped environment (MountainCar-v0).

Incomplete presentation and reporting: Several plots lack clear uncertainty quantification (e.g., standard error/deviation bands across independent seeds), and key implementation details (such as runtime per episode and exact compute scaling) are absent from the main text.

strengths: Original and creative conceptual idea: repurposing an in-context tabular foundation model (TabPFN) as a non-parametric Q-function regressor within Fitted Q-Iteration (FQI), eliminating gradient-based parameter updates during policy learning.

Insightful conceptual discussion regarding task-prior mismatch: the authors explicitly articulate the theoretical tension between TabPFN's meta-training distribution (i.i.d. tabular data) and the reality of RL (bootstrapped non-i.i.d. targets, temporal dependencies, and non-stationary visitation shifts).

Exploration of context management: the paper systematically formulates and evaluates several heuristic truncation strategies (naive de-duplication, representation de-duplication, and reward variance filtering) to address the finite context window constraint inherent to in-context RL.
weaknesses: Narrow and heavily modified empirical evaluation: the method is tested on only three low-dimensional classic control tasks (CartPole-v1, MountainCar-v0, Acrobot-v1). Crucially, the authors apply custom reward shaping to all three tasks to make rewards dense (Appendix), leaving it completely unverified whether the method can operate under standard benchmark reward specifications or scale beyond trivial state spaces.

Lack of appropriate baselines and runtime comparison: the only comparison provided is against a standard DQN. Crucial baselines are absent, including classical gradient-free methods (e.g., ARS, CMA-ES), nearest-neighbor RL, and especially standard non-parametric FQI variants (such as Extra-Trees FQI / Random Forests), which are also gradient-free and tabular. Furthermore, despite claiming computational efficiency, running 60 iterations of transformer forward passes over contexts of up to several thousand tokens during online interaction introduces massive inference overhead; no wall-clock or compute-cost comparisons are provided.

Underspecification of the inner TabPFN-FQI loop: the algorithmic details of how TabPFN evaluates Bellman targets across the 60 FQI iterations are omitted in the main text. Specifically, computing $\max_{a'} Q(s'_i, a')$ across the dataset requires repeated transformer forward passes for every candidate action at every iteration; the computational pipeline and its exact batching/caching mechanics need much clearer description.

Statistical reporting: in Figure 1, curves are presented with minimal or poorly resolved confidence bands, and aggregate metrics (e.g., interquartile mean or performance profiles over multiple runs) recommended by standard RL evaluation protocols are missing.

strengths: The core conceptual idea of repurposing pre-trained tabular in-context regression (ICR) foundation models (such as TabPFN) as value function approximators via Fitted Q-Iteration (FQI) without gradient updates or RL-specific pre-training is creative and intriguing.

The paper identifies the critical context-length bottleneck in transformer-based agents and systematically proposes and compares several context-engineering strategies (e.g., Naive De-duplication, Embedding De-duplication, Reward Variance) to maintain informative replay data under fixed token budgets.

The discussion in Section 5 transparently articulates the fundamental mismatch between the i.i.d. pre-training assumptions of tabular foundation models and the non-stationary, correlated, bootstrapped distribution shifts intrinsic to RL.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is extremely restricted, limited to only three low-dimensional classic control benchmarks (CartPole-v1, MountainCar-v0, and Acrobot-v1). These toy environments do not sufficiently demonstrate the viability or scalability of ICR-RL for modern reinforcement learning.

The method relies heavily on bespoke reward shaping (detailed in Appendix B.2) to establish learning. As acknowledged by the authors, the approach struggles under standard sparse reward formulations, which significantly compromises its claim of zero-shot general-purpose applicability.

The baseline comparisons over a short horizon (250 episodes) appear suboptimal and potentially undertuned. For example, standard PPO and TRPO implementations typically master CartPole-v1 (achieving the maximum return of 500) rapidly, yet in Figure 2 PPO plateaus around 100 reward, suggesting poor baseline tuning or artifacts of the custom reward shaping.

Inference latency and computational overhead remain severe concerns. Because action selection at each environment step requires evaluating all candidate actions across the context dataset, and ICR-FQI requires repeated forward passes across the entire context buffer for $K$ iterations, the practical wall-clock and inference cost per step is substantially higher than standard gradient-based parametric methods.

The theoretical grounding of FQI convergence breaks down in practice with the chosen ICR model. In Section C.1 and Figure 8, the authors observe that increasing the number of iterations toward the theoretical fixed-point requirement ($K \approx \frac{1}{1-\gamma}$) degrades performance, showing that the black-box regressor exhibits instability under recursive bootstrapping.

strengths: Interesting conceptual angle: connecting general-purpose tabular in-context regression models (e.g., TabPFN, TabICL) to reinforcement learning via the classical Fitted Q Iteration (FQI) reduction without gradient updates.

The paper explicitly identifies and analyzes the problem of context management/context exhaustion in in-context RL, proposing sensible heuristics (such as distance-based deduplication and reward-variance filtering).

Clear writing, easy-to-follow explanations of the reduction to FQI, and thoughtful discussion of the distributional mismatch between i.i.d. tabular pretraining data and sequential, non-stationary RL trajectories.
weaknesses: Extremely limited empirical evaluation: The method is evaluated exclusively on three toy classical control environments (CartPole-v1, MountainCar-v0, and Acrobot-v1) for a very short duration (250–300 episodes). These low-dimensional tasks do not provide sufficient evidence of practical utility or scalability to modern RL benchmarks (e.g., MuJoCo, Brax, MinAtar, or Atari).

Heavy dependence on manual reward shaping: As acknowledged in Section 4 and detailed in Appendix B.2, the method fails on sparse-reward tasks and requires hand-crafted dense potential/distance-based reward shaping for all evaluated environments. This substantially narrows the applicability and obscures the true algorithmic capability compared to standard RL formulations.

Baselines appear severely under-tuned or anomalous: In Figure 2, standard algorithms like PPO and TRPO fail to solve CartPole-v1 (achieving returns under 100 after 250 episodes, whereas standard PPO implementations readily reach the maximum reward of 500 within tens of thousands of steps). Such poorly performing baselines make the claimed superiority over policy gradient methods unconvincing.

High computational and memory overhead without direct wall-clock comparison: Evaluating action values at every environment step by passing the entire context and query set through a full transformer architecture is computationally demanding and quadratic in context length. While Figure 5 shows normalized runtimes comparing different context-retention heuristics, the paper lacks absolute wall-clock runtime comparisons against the standard gradient-based baselines (e.g., DQN/PPO), which typically run orders of magnitude faster.

Limited algorithmic novelty: The proposed framework directly replaces the standard regression function in classical FQI with an existing off-the-shelf tabular regression model (TabPFN). Beyond combining existing components and applying standard geometric deduplication heuristics, the core methodological contribution is modest.

strengths: Original and intriguing conceptual framing: reducing reinforcement learning value estimation to In-Context Regression (ICR) using pre-trained tabular foundation models (such as TabPFN) without any RL-specific pre-training or gradient updates.

The manuscript identifies and clearly discusses the theoretical challenges and task-prior mismatches when applying i.i.d. tabular models to RL, specifically non-stationary bootstrapping, temporal correlations, and distribution shift.

Recognizes the quadratic memory/compute bottleneck of transformers and investigates practical context engineering heuristics (such as naive deduplication) to maintain a bounded context buffer for continual learning.
weaknesses: Extremely limited empirical evaluation: Experiments are restricted to three classic control environments (CartPole-v1, MountainCar-v0, Acrobot-v1). There is no evaluation on higher-dimensional tasks, standard continuous control benchmarks (e.g., MuJoCo/Gymnasium robotics), or standard offline/online RL benchmarks.

Heavy reliance on dense reward shaping: The authors acknowledge that ICR-RL fails or struggles under default sparse reward settings (requiring custom reward shaping as detailed in Appendix B.2). This significantly limits the generality and real-world applicability of the approach.

Questionable baseline performance: Standard policy gradient baselines (PPO and TRPO) exhibit abnormally poor performance on toy tasks like CartPole-v1 (e.g., PPO failing to achieve maximum return within 250 episodes, whereas standard implementations easily solve unshaped CartPole in under 100 episodes). It appears the baselines were evaluated under suboptimal hyperparameter configurations or penalized by the custom reward shaping.

Computational overhead and inference latency: At every single environment step, ICR-RL evaluates all actions via forward passes through the full context buffer, and multiple iterative Bellman refitting passes are performed whenever an episode is accepted into the context. The paper provides normalized execution times across context sizes, but lacks absolute wall-clock latency comparisons against standard RL baselines.
